etymology: A portmanteau of robots and blocks. Built by David Baszucki and Erik Cassel, beta-tested in 2004 as DynaBlocks, renamed in 2005, and launched publicly in 2006. Roblox is not one game but a platform of millions of user-made "experiences" written in Roblox Studio, most of them free to enter and paid for by in-game purchases. By 2025 it counted more than a hundred million users a day, a large share of them children under thirteen, and "Can I play Roblox?" became the most-asked question in the American Gen Alpha household.
biblical_def: To a Gen Alpha child, Roblox is less a game than a place: the playground, mall, and clubhouse where friends meet after school, where they build, trade, role-play, and play other children’s games. To say "I was on Roblox" is to say "I was out" — in a town made by strangers, open to strangers. The Christian observation: the urge underneath is good. God made man a maker and put him in a garden "to dress it and to keep it" (Gen 2:15), and He filled Bezaleel "with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding" for "all manner of workmanship" (Exo 31:3). A child who builds an obstacle course in Roblox Studio is showing the image of the Creator in miniature. But a place is only as safe as its gatekeepers, and Roblox’s gate is a chat box and a price tag. Scripture tells a father to keep the door of his home and his child’s eyes: "I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes" (Psa 101:3), and "keep thy heart with all diligence" (Pro 4:23). A father can tell a five-year-old: "God made you to build things, just like He builds. We build together, and Daddy always knows who is in the room with you." And he can tell himself: redeem the time (Eph 5:16); a child’s afternoons are a stewardship, not a babysitter.
webster_summary: Gen Alpha’s defining game platform (launched 2006): a world of user-made games and hangouts — the child’s maker-instinct, which is God’s gift, opened onto a marketplace and a chat box that need a father at the door.
webster_full: ROBLOX, proper n. (Gen Alpha usage, c. 2015–present; platform launched 2006) The online game platform of user-built "experiences"; by extension, the after-school social world itself. "Everyone’s on Roblox tonight."
Used as a place-name rather than a title: one is "on Roblox," "in a Roblox game," "meeting on Roblox."
Related terms: Robux (its currency), obby (obstacle course), experience (the platform’s word for a game), Roblox Studio (the free building tool).
Decode for parents: your child is not playing one game; she is visiting thousands of strangers’ games, with chat, trading, and purchases built in.
Webster 1828, the root — BLOCK, n. A heavy piece of timber or wood, usually with one plain surface; or it is rectangular, and rather thick than long.
scriptures: And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship,
I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me.
Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
corruption_summary: Roblox takes the God-given urge to make and to gather and sells it back as a stranger-run town with a cash register at every door; the gift is real, the gatekeeping belongs to the father.
corruption_paragraphs: The platform’s genius is that children make the games, and the platform’s danger is the same fact. A world built by millions of anonymous hands has no single author to answer for it, so the child meets whatever the last builder thought was funny, and whoever happens to be in the chat. The economy is designed so that the free door leads quickly to a paid one. That is the pattern Scripture warns a householder about: an open gate and a watchman asleep.

Yet the instinct the platform harvests is holy. Man was put in a garden to dress it; Bezaleel was filled with the Spirit for workmanship. A Christian father need not treat building as a vice; he can redeem it by building with his child, keeping the gate (privacy settings, friends he knows, no strangers’ chat), and pointing the work back to the One who "created the heavens and the earth." Teach her that she is a maker because her Father is the Maker — and that a good maker builds in the light.
roots_summary: Robots + blocks → DynaBlocks (2004 beta) → Roblox (2005–06) → Gen Alpha’s after-school town (2015–present).
roots_lines: English robot (from Czech robota, forced labour; Karel Capek, 1920) + block (the toy brick)
2004: DynaBlocks, the beta built by David Baszucki and Erik Cassel
2005–2006: renamed and launched as Roblox
2010s: Roblox Studio makes every player a potential game-maker; the platform’s word becomes "experience"
2020s: Gen Alpha’s default social space, past a hundred million daily users
usage: "Mom, can I get on Roblox with Ava? We’re building a house."
Roblox harvests the maker-instinct God gave; the father keeps the gate of the garden (Gen 2:15).
A child’s afternoon on Roblox is a stewardship of time to redeem, not a sitter to rent (Eph 5:16).

etymology: Roblox’s virtual currency, a blend of Roblox and bucks. Introduced in 2007 alongside a free earnable currency called Tix, which Roblox retired in 2016, leaving Robux — bought with real money — as the only coin of the realm. It buys avatar clothing, accessories, game passes, and in-game advantages; creators can cash Robux out through the Developer Exchange. "Can I have Robux?" became the standard Gen Alpha birthday wish and the standard Gen Alpha plea at the checkout lane, usually by the gift card.
biblical_def: Robux is the money of Roblox, and to a child it is money in the fullest sense: the thing that buys belonging. A child with no Robux wears the default look and cannot buy the pass; a child with Robux can look like everyone else, or better. "How much Robux do you have?" is a playground census of status. The Christian observation: the Bible is not shy about money, and it is not fooled by it. "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also" (Mat 6:21). The coin may be digital, but the heart that wants it is the same heart that wanted Achan’s wedge of gold. Scripture teaches children to work, to give, and to be content: "godliness with contentment is great gain" (1Ti 6:6), and the treasure that lasts is laid up "in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt" (Mat 6:20) — nor any server shut down. Robux can be a good teacher if a father uses it: a child who earns her Robux by chores learns that money is the fruit of labor (Pro 13:11) and that a dollar spent on a hat is a dollar not given. A father can tell a five-year-old: "Robux is pretend money that costs real money. Jesus says the best treasure is the kind you keep in heaven — like being kind and giving to others."
webster_summary: Roblox’s real-money virtual currency (2007; sole currency since 2016) — the child’s first economy of status, where Scripture’s teaching on treasure, labor, and contentment can be learned early or ignored early.
webster_full: ROBUX, n. (Gen Alpha slang, c. 2015–present; currency introduced 2007) The purchasable virtual currency of Roblox, spent on avatar items and game passes. "I need 400 Robux for the pass."
Often abbreviated R$; bought by card or gift card in fixed bundles.
Free Robux — the bait phrase of scams promising currency for a password (see the entry).
Decode for parents: Robux is real money in a costume; what it mostly buys is how your child looks to other children.
scriptures: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
But godliness with contentment is great gain.
Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase.
Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
corruption_summary: Robux trains a child to buy belonging; Scripture trains her to lay up treasure in heaven, to eat the fruit of her own labor, and to be content.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is not that the currency is digital but that it is a currency of appearance. Most Robux goes to how an avatar looks, and so the child learns early that worth can be purchased and displayed. That is the oldest economy of the fallen heart — "the pride of life" — in its first, cartoon form. Children who beg for Robux are not unusually greedy; they are simply being honest about a world that prices status.

A Christian household can turn the currency into a classroom. Let Robux be earned, not owed; let a tithe come out of the first allowance before the first hat is bought; let contentment be praised aloud when a child chooses not to spend. "Be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee" (Heb 13:5). A child who learns that lesson over a digital hat has learned it for the mortgage.
roots_summary: Roblox + bucks → Robux (2007) → sole Roblox currency after Tix retired (2016) → Gen Alpha’s playground economy.
roots_lines: American English buck — a dollar (from the frontier deerskin trade)
2007: Robux introduced on Roblox beside earnable Tix
2016: Tix retired; Robux, bought with real money, becomes the only currency
Developer Exchange: creators convert earned Robux to cash
2020s: gift-card aisle staple; "How much Robux do you have?" as status census
usage: "Grandma got me a Robux card! I’m buying the dragon wings."
Where your Robux is, there will your heart be also (Mat 6:21).
Let her earn it with chores, and tithe the first ten percent — a Robux lesson is a mortgage lesson in miniature.

etymology: Clipped from obstacle course with the diminutive -y. The obby is Roblox’s oldest and most popular game genre: a run of jumps, moving platforms, lava floors, and spinning bars, with checkpoints so a fall sends you back only partway. Tower of Hell (2018) and countless "Escape the ___ Obby" games made the word universal on the playground by the late 2010s; children now build their own obbies in Roblox Studio and dare friends to beat them.
biblical_def: An obby is an obstacle course, and Gen Alpha children love them for the same reason children always have: falling, trying again, and finally making it to the end. The checkpoint is the obby’s mercy — you do not start over from the beginning every time you fall. The Christian observation: this is one of the redeemable words, because it carries a picture Scripture itself uses. The Christian life is a course to run with endurance: "let us run with patience the race that is set before us, looking unto Jesus" (Heb 12:1-2). Paul did not pretend he had already finished: "I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus" (Php 3:14). And the man who falls is not finished: "a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Pro 24:16). The obby’s checkpoint is a small picture of grace — God does not send His child back to the start when he stumbles. A father can tell a five-year-old: "Life is like an obby. You’ll fall sometimes. Jesus helps you get back up, and He’s waiting at the finish." And to the older child who rage-quits a hard level: "Ye have need of patience" (Heb 10:36); the course is the training.
webster_summary: Roblox’s obstacle-course genre (clip of obstacle course; universal by the late 2010s) — a redeemable picture of the race set before us, the fall-and-rise of the just, and the mercy of the checkpoint.
webster_full: OBBY, n. (Gen Alpha slang, 2010s–present) A Roblox obstacle course of jumps, hazards, and checkpoints. "Can you beat my obby?"
Common forms: "Escape the ___ Obby," "tower obby," "difficulty chart obby." To make an obby is a child’s first game design.
Checkpoint — the save-point that returns a fallen player partway, not to the start.
Decode for parents: one of the cleaner corners of Roblox, and a ready-made sermon illustration about perseverance.
Webster 1828, the root — OBSTACLE, n. That which opposes; any thing that stands in the way and hinders progress; hinderance; obstruction, either in a physical or moral sense.
scriptures: Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief.
For ye have need of patience, that, after ye have done the will of God, ye might receive the promise.
Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain.
corruption_summary: The obby is mostly innocent play; its only corruption is the impatience that quits at the hard jump, and Scripture answers it with the race run in patience and the just man who rises seven times.
corruption_paragraphs: Little is wrong with an obstacle course. The risks are the platform’s, not the genre’s: an obby can be a doorway to purchases ("skip stage for 25 Robux") and to the habit of paying to avoid difficulty. That is worth naming, because the skip-stage button teaches the opposite of the course itself — that struggle is a thing to buy your way out of.

Redeem the word by using it. Paul’s race (1Co 9:24), Hebrews’ cloud of witnesses, and the just man who falls seven times are all obby-shaped. Praise the child who keeps trying more than the child who wins; tell her the checkpoint is how God’s patience works — "his compassions fail not. They are new every morning" (Lam 3:22-23). A course you are allowed to finish is a mercy.
roots_summary: Obstacle course → obby (Roblox genre, 2000s–2010s) → Tower of Hell (2018) and the child-made obby.
roots_lines: Latin obstaculum (from obstare, to stand in the way) → English obstacle
Military and playground obstacle course (20th c.)
Roblox clipping obby, the platform’s oldest genre
2018: Tower of Hell popularizes the no-checkpoint climb
2020s: "Escape the ___ Obby" and kid-built obbies everywhere
usage: "I’m on stage 47 of the obby and I keep falling in the lava!"
The obby is a picture of Hebrews 12: run with patience, eyes on the finish.
A just man falleth seven times and riseth up again — tell her that at stage 47 (Pro 24:16).

etymology: From the default brown hairstyle (officially "Pal Hair") given to new male Roblox avatars from the late 2010s, whose wavy strands look like strips of bacon. Because only new or non-paying players wore it, bacon hair became shorthand on Roblox for a newcomer, a beginner, or a poor kid with no Robux to buy a better look; the female default look got its own nicknames. The bacon-hair player became a meme character in his own right — the underdog noob who sometimes turns out to be a pro.
biblical_def: To call someone a bacon hair on Roblox is to call him a newbie, a nobody, or a kid whose parents did not buy him Robux — you can tell by the free haircut. It is a playground class label: the default look marks you as poor or new, and the children who have paid for better avatars sometimes mock or exclude the ones who have not. The Christian observation: this is the sin James names with startling precision. If a man comes into the assembly "with a gold ring, in goodly apparel," and a poor man "in vile raiment," and you say to the rich man "sit thou here in a good place" and to the poor man "stand thou there" — "are ye not then partial in yourselves?" (Jas 2:2-4). Scripture says God "hath chosen the poor of this world rich in faith" (Jas 2:5), and that "the LORD looketh on the heart" (1Sa 16:7). The bacon hair is the child God tells us to sit beside. A father can tell a five-year-old: "God doesn’t care what your avatar wears. If someone has the free hair, you be extra kind to him — that’s what Jesus did." The meme’s own twist — the bacon hair who turns out to be the best player — is a small parable of the last who shall be first (Mat 20:16).
webster_summary: Roblox nickname for a default-avatar newcomer or non-paying player (late 2010s) — a cartoon class label that Scripture rebukes as respect of persons.
webster_full: BACON HAIR, n. (Gen Alpha slang, late 2010s–present) A Roblox player wearing the free default hairstyle; hence, a beginner, noob, or player without Robux. "Some bacon hair just beat me."
Used both as a sneer and, increasingly, affectionately — the bacon-hair underdog is a stock meme hero.
Decode for parents: listen for whether your child uses it to mock; it is a status word about money.
Webster 1828, the root — BACON, n. Hog’s flesh, salted or pickled and dried, usually in smoke.
scriptures: For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment;
Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts?
Hearken, my beloved brethren, Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him?

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen.
corruption_summary: Bacon hair sorts children by what their avatars cost; Scripture calls that respect of persons and seats the poor man in the good place.
corruption_paragraphs: Children learn class early, and digital worlds make it visible: the purchased look versus the free one. Bacon hair is the word that names the free one, and in the mouth of a child who has Robux it can carry exactly the contempt James condemns — the gold ring seated, the vile raiment made to stand. It is a small sin in pixels and a large one in a heart that is being trained.

The meme’s best version redeems itself: the bacon-hair noob who wins, the plain kid who is kind. Teach your child to love that version. Christ came not in goodly apparel but as one with "no form nor comeliness" (Isa 53:2), and He made friends with the overlooked. A child who sits beside the bacon hair is doing what his Lord did.
roots_summary: Default Roblox "Pal Hair" (looks like bacon) → bacon hair = new or non-paying player → underdog meme hero.
roots_lines: Old French bacon → English bacon, cured pork
Late 2010s Roblox default male hairstyle, wavy brown strands
Playground extension: newcomer, noob, kid with no Robux
Meme figure: the bacon-hair underdog who turns out to be a pro
usage: "Don’t kick him from the server just ‘cause he’s a bacon hair."
James 2 in a Roblox lobby: the paid avatar seated, the bacon hair made to stand.
The last shall be first — even the bacon hair (Mat 20:16).

etymology: An imitative grunt of mild pain or dismay, older than the internet, made iconic for Gen Alpha by Roblox’s character death sound — a short "uuhh" played every time an avatar fell apart, from the platform’s early years until 2022. Players called it "the oof sound," and "oof" became the universal kid response to any small disaster. The sound was traced to sound-design work for the 2000 PC game Messiah; after a licensing dispute Roblox replaced it in July 2022, and a generation mourned it in memes.
biblical_def: Oof is what a Gen Alpha kid says when something goes slightly wrong — a spilled cup, a bad grade, a friend’s embarrassing moment. It means "ouch" with a shrug, sympathy and amusement at once. The word is mostly harmless, and a household can use it freely. The Christian observation: what matters is whose pain you are "oofing" at. Said with sympathy, it is a small way to "weep with them that weep" (Rom 12:15) — a word that notices another’s trouble. Said with a smirk at someone’s fall, it becomes the laugh Scripture forbids: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth" (Pro 24:17). The difference is the heart, and a child can learn it. A father can tell a five-year-old: "When somebody falls down, we can say ‘oof’ — and then we help them up." That is the Samaritan’s order: see, feel, then go to him (Luk 10:33-34). And a child who says "oof" at her own little disasters can learn the larger lesson that "all things work together for good to them that love God" (Rom 8:28) — an oof is never the last word.
webster_summary: Imitative interjection of mild pain or sympathy, made iconic by Roblox’s death sound (until 2022) — neutral, and good when it notices another’s trouble rather than mocking it.
webster_full: OOF, interj. (old imitative grunt; Gen Alpha iconic via Roblox, 2010s–present) An expression of mild pain, dismay, or sympathy. "Oof, you got a C?"
The oof sound — Roblox’s original avatar death sound, replaced in July 2022.
Big oof — intensified: a serious embarrassment or setback.
Decode for parents: harmless; listen only for whether it is sympathy or a sneer.
scriptures: Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth:
But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him,
And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.
corruption_summary: Oof is a neutral grunt; it sins only when it laughs at a neighbor’s fall instead of weeping with him.
corruption_paragraphs: There is little to correct in a word this small. Its one hazard is the reflexive delight in other people’s mishaps that internet culture rewards — the fail video, the clip of someone tripping. When oof becomes the soundtrack of that, it is the gladness at a stumble that Proverbs warns against, and the mockery that "the seat of the scornful" invites (Psa 1:1).

Keep the word and train the heart behind it. Make "oof" the first half of a sentence whose second half is help. The Good Samaritan saw, had compassion, and went to him. A family that answers every small disaster with sympathy first is teaching the oldest manners in the Bible.
roots_summary: Imitative grunt of pain (long-standing English) → Roblox "oof" death sound (2000s–2022) → universal Gen Alpha interjection.
roots_lines: Imitative English grunt of a blow to the stomach, attested in comics and speech for generations
Roblox avatar death sound, the "oof," from the platform’s early years
Traced to sound-design work on the 2000 game Messiah
July 2022: replaced after a licensing dispute; memorialized in memes
Big oof — intensified form
usage: "Oof — you dropped your whole ice cream. Want some of mine?"
An oof of sympathy weeps with them that weep (Rom 12:15); an oof of glee rejoices when another falleth (Pro 24:17).
See, feel, then help: the Samaritan’s oof (Luk 10:33-34).

etymology: The bait phrase of the most common scam aimed at Gen Alpha. From the late 2010s, YouTube comments, TikTok videos, fake websites, and in-game messages promised "FREE ROBUX" through a "generator" — in exchange for a username and password, a survey, a downloaded app, or a parent’s card. No such generator exists; the payoff is a stolen account, malware, or a charge on Mom’s card. Roblox’s own help pages warn that there is no free-Robux generator. Kids now say "free Robux" ironically for anything too good to be true.
biblical_def: Free Robux is the promise of something for nothing, and every child who has played Roblox has seen it: a flashing video, a too-friendly stranger, a website that wants just your password. It is the first con most Gen Alpha children ever meet, and some of them learn its lesson the hard way, losing an account they spent years on. The Christian observation: this is a perfect first lesson in the Ninth and Eighth Commandments and in the wisdom of Proverbs. "The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going" (Pro 14:15). The scammer is the man who "lieth in wait secretly as a lion in his den" to "catch the poor" (Psa 10:9), and Scripture’s verdict on him is plain: "Thou shalt not steal" (Exo 20:15). But it is also a lesson about the bait in the child’s own heart — the wish to get without earning. "He that hasteth to be rich hath an evil eye, and considereth not that poverty shall come upon him" (Pro 28:22). A father can tell a five-year-old: "If someone says ‘free Robux,’ it’s a trick, like the wolf in the fairy tale. Never tell anyone your password — only Mommy and Daddy." And later: the only truly free gift is the one God gives — "the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord" (Rom 6:23) — and it never asks for your password.
webster_summary: The bait phrase of Roblox account-theft and phishing scams (late 2010s–present) — the child’s first meeting with the liar who lies in wait, and with the get-without-earning wish Proverbs warns against.
webster_full: FREE ROBUX, n. phr. (Gen Alpha slang, late 2010s–present) The false promise of free Roblox currency used to steal accounts, passwords, or payment details. "That free Robux site is a scam."
Ironic extension: anything too good to be true. "Free iPad? Sounds like free Robux."
Variants: Robux generator, free Robux codes, Robux giveaway — all bait.
Decode for parents: teach the rule before the scam teaches it — no password, ever, to anyone outside the family.
Webster 1828, the root — FREE, a. Being at liberty; not being under necessity or restraint, physical or moral; a word of general application to the body, the will or mind, and to corporations.
scriptures: The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going.
He lieth in wait secretly as a lion in his den: he lieth in wait to catch the poor: he doth catch the poor, when he draweth him into his net.
He that hasteth to be rich hath an evil eye, and considereth not that poverty shall come upon him.
For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
corruption_summary: Free Robux is a liar’s lure that works on a child’s wish to get without earning; Scripture names the thief, warns the simple, and points to the one gift that is truly free.
corruption_paragraphs: Two sins meet in this phrase. On one side is the scammer, who studies children’s desires in order to rob them — the lion in his den of Psalm 10. On the other side is the child’s own covetous hope that wealth can come without work. The con succeeds because the second sin opens the door to the first. That is why Proverbs pairs prudence with contentment: the man who is not hasting to be rich is hard to trick.

Make the scam a catechism. Teach the password rule as a household law; teach that "too good to be true" is usually a lie; and teach the deeper truth that there is a free gift — grace — which costs the giver everything and the receiver nothing, and which never needs to be guarded behind a login. A child who knows the real free gift is less hungry for the fake one.
roots_summary: Late-2010s phishing bait ("free Robux generator") → account theft and card fraud → ironic shorthand for anything too good to be true.
roots_lines: Old English freo — not in bondage; given without cost
Late 2010s: "free Robux generator" sites, videos, and in-game messages
The payoff: stolen accounts, malware, unauthorized charges
Roblox help pages: there is no free-Robux generator
Ironic kid usage: "sounds like free Robux" = a scam
usage: "Some guy said he’d give me free Robux if I told him my password — I said no!"
The simple believeth every word; the prudent child keeps her password (Pro 14:15).
The only real free gift never asks for your login (Rom 6:23).

etymology: From American scam (a swindle; mid-20th century, origin uncertain, possibly carnival slang). Gen Alpha’s version is rooted in Roblox and Adopt Me! trading culture of the late 2010s and 2020s, where children trade rare pets and limited items and some trades are rigged: the "trust trade" (you give first, I’ll give after), the switched item, the fake middleman. "SCAMMER!" became the most serious accusation a child can make in a game, and also a teasing word among siblings for anyone who breaks a deal.
biblical_def: On a Gen Alpha playground a scammer is anyone who cheats you in a trade — in a game, or with Pokemon cards, or over the last cookie. Children feel scams with a fierce sense of justice, which is good: they know instinctively that a broken bargain is wrong. The Christian observation: Scripture shares the child’s outrage. "A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight" (Pro 11:1). The man who "sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not" is the one who may dwell in God’s holy hill (Psa 15:4) — that is, the person who keeps a deal even when it costs him. But the child who shouts "scammer!" also needs the other half of the lesson: the same justice applies to her. "Defraud not" is a command for everyone (Mar 10:19), and Zacchaeus shows what repentance looks like for a cheat — "if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold" (Luk 19:8). A father can tell a five-year-old: "A scammer breaks a promise to get something. God always keeps His promises — so we keep ours, even in games." And when his child gets scammed, he can model the hardest part: "Recompense to no man evil for evil" (Rom 12:17).
webster_summary: Roblox and Adopt Me! trading slang for one who cheats in a trade (late 2010s–present) — a child’s sense of justice Scripture affirms, and turns back on the accuser too.
webster_full: SCAMMER, n. (Gen Alpha usage, late 2010s–present, from Roblox trading) One who cheats another in a trade or deal. "He took my neon unicorn and left — total scammer."
Common scams named by kids: trust trade, fake middleman, switch, free Robux.
Teasing use among siblings: anyone who breaks a bargain.
Decode for parents: your child is learning economics and justice at once; teach both.
scriptures: A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.
Thou knowest the commandments, Do not commit adultery, Do not kill, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Defraud not, Honour thy father and mother.
And Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord; Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold.
Recompense to no man evil for evil. Provide things honest in the sight of all men.
corruption_summary: The scammer breaks faith for gain, and children rightly hate him; Scripture agrees, then requires the accuser to keep faith too and to return no evil for evil.
corruption_paragraphs: Children’s trading games are a small market, and every market is a school of honesty or of fraud. The scammer is the merchant of the false balance in miniature, and Scripture’s hatred of the false balance is constant from Leviticus to Micah. When a child is cheated in Adopt Me!, she has met a real moral reality, not a trivial one, and her anger is a sign that the law is written on her heart (Rom 2:15).

The danger is that the word becomes only an accusation, never a mirror. Teach the child who cries "scammer" to keep her own trades straight, to make restitution like Zacchaeus when she is wrong, and to refuse revenge-scams. A household that keeps its word in games is training children who keep vows at the altar.
roots_summary: American scam (swindle, mid-20th c.) + -er → Roblox and Adopt Me! trading accusation (late 2010s–2020s).
roots_lines: American English scam — a swindle (mid-20th c.; origin uncertain)
Scammer — one who runs a scam
Late 2010s: Roblox and Adopt Me! pet and item trading
Named techniques: trust trade, fake middleman, item switch
Playground extension: anyone who breaks a deal
usage: "Don’t trust-trade with him. He’s a scammer."
A false balance is abomination to the LORD — even in Adopt Me! (Pro 11:1).
Keep your trade though it cost you; that is Psalm 15:4 in a Roblox lobby.

etymology: Clipped from administrator, the person who runs a server, forum, or game. In Roblox, an admin has commands that others lack — fly, kick, ban, spawn items, change the weather — and "admin" games and "free admin" servers let children taste that power. In 2025 the hit Roblox game Grow a Garden made "admin abuse" a scheduled event: the developers logged in on weekends to shower players with rare seeds and weather, and millions crowded in to be there when the admin showed up. To a Gen Alpha child, the admin is the one with all the power in the room.
biblical_def: To a Gen Alpha child an admin is the player with god-mode: he can fly, kick you, ban you, or rain rare items on everyone. Children both fear and adore the admin, and "admin abuse" means either a cruel use of power (kicking people for fun) or, in Grow a Garden’s case, a generous shower of gifts. The Christian observation: the word is a ready-made lesson on authority. All earthly power is borrowed: "there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God" (Rom 13:1). The admin who kicks players for fun is the ruler who "lord[s] it over" others, and Jesus says plainly, "it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister" (Mat 20:25-26). And the admin who logs in to pour out gifts on a crowd is a faint picture of the true Lord who "giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not" (Jas 1:5) and who "maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good" (Mat 5:45). A father can tell a five-year-old: "God is the real Admin of everything — and He uses His power to help us, not to be mean. When you get to be in charge, you do the same."
webster_summary: Clipped administrator: the in-game holder of god-mode commands; "admin abuse" = cruel or (Grow a Garden, 2025) generous use of that power — a picture of authority as stewardship under God.
webster_full: ADMIN, n. (computing clip of administrator; Gen Alpha game usage, 2010s–present) The player or developer with special commands in a game or server. "The admin just banned him."
Admin abuse — (1) using admin power cruelly; (2) Grow a Garden (2025): a scheduled developer event showering players with gifts.
Free admin — a server where every player may use admin commands.
Decode for parents: your child is learning what power does to people — an open door to talk about authority.

Webster 1828, the root — ADMINISTRATOR, n. a man who, by virtue of a commission from the Ordinary, Surrogate, Court of Probate, or other proper authority, has the charge of the goods and estate of one dying without a will.
scriptures: Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them.
But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;
If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.
That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.
corruption_summary: The admin holds borrowed power; used for cruelty it is the Gentile lordship Jesus forbids, used for gifts it faintly pictures the Lord who gives liberally.
corruption_paragraphs: Children in game worlds meet raw power for the first time: someone who can erase you from the room with a word. The admin who kicks for fun is a small tyrant, and children who get admin commands often become one immediately. That is the oldest story of the fallen heart — Lamech boasting of vengeance, Rehoboam’s whips into scorpions. Power reveals.

Use the word to teach servant authority. All power is ordained of God and answerable to Him; the greatest among you is the minister. When your child gets "admin" in a game — or gets put in charge of a younger sibling — ask what he will do with it. The admin worth imitating is the one who logs in to give.
roots_summary: Latin administrare (to serve, manage) → English administrator → computing admin → Roblox god-mode player; Grow a Garden "admin abuse" (2025).
roots_lines: Latin ad + ministrare, to serve, attend, manage
English administrator — one who manages affairs
Late 20th c. computing: admin, the system operator
Roblox: admin commands (fly, kick, ban, spawn)
2025: Grow a Garden’s weekend "admin abuse" gift events
usage: "The admin’s on! He’s giving everybody rainbow seeds!"
The word itself says minister: whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister (Mat 20:26).
God is the true Admin, and He uses His power to give (Jas 1:5).

etymology: From English ban (to forbid, to curse; Old English bannan, to summon or proclaim). In game culture, to be banned is to be removed from a game or platform by its moderators or admins, temporarily or for good. For Gen Alpha, "you’re gonna get banned" and "I’ll get you banned" are the ultimate playground threats, and the "ban hammer" is a meme image of judgment. Roblox’s moderation bans accounts for rule-breaking, and children’s anxiety about losing years of progress makes the word carry real weight.
biblical_def: In Gen Alpha usage, banned means kicked out of a game for good — your account, your items, your friends list, gone. Children fear it more than almost any other in-game consequence, and they use the threat freely: "Stop or I’ll report you and you’ll get banned." The Christian observation: the word carries, without knowing it, the shape of one of Scripture’s heaviest themes — exclusion from the presence of the Lord. Adam and Eve were driven out of the garden, and "at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword" kept the way (Gen 3:24). The final ban is real: "there shall in no wise enter into it any thing that defileth" (Rev 21:27). But the gospel is the news that the banned can be brought back. "But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ" (Eph 2:13), and Jesus promises, "him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out" (Joh 6:37). A father can tell a five-year-old: "When we did wrong, we deserved to be banned from God’s house. But Jesus took our punishment, so now the door is open. He never bans anyone who comes to Him." And to the child threatening to get a playmate banned: love "thinketh no evil" (1Co 13:5); go to your brother first (Mat 18:15).
webster_summary: Removed from a game or platform by its moderators — Gen Alpha’s ultimate threat, and an accidental picture of exclusion from God’s presence and of the gospel that brings the banned near.
webster_full: BANNED, a. / pp. (gaming usage; Gen Alpha, 2010s–present) Removed from a game, server, or platform by moderators or admins. "He got banned for exploiting."
Ban hammer — the meme image of moderator judgment; perma-ban — permanent removal; temp-ban — temporary.
Playground threat: "I’ll get you banned."
Decode for parents: losing an account feels to a child like exile; take the fear seriously and use it to talk about the gospel.
Webster 1828, the root — BAN, n. A public proclamation or edict; a public order or notice, mandatory or prohibitory.
scriptures: So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.
And there shall in no wise enter into it any thing that defileth, neither whatsoever worketh abomination, or maketh a lie: but they which are written in the Lamb's book of life.
But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.
corruption_summary: To be banned is exile from the game; Scripture knows a worse exile and a better welcome, and forbids the child to wield the ban as a weapon on his brother.
corruption_paragraphs: The fear of being banned is real, and so is the pleasure of threatening it. A child who learns that reporting can remove a rival from the room has learned a dangerous power, and "I’ll get you banned" is often spite dressed as justice. Scripture’s order is different: go to your brother alone first; only then bring witnesses; only at the end, "tell it unto the church" (Mat 18:15-17). Exclusion is a last resort of love, never a first resort of anger.

The deeper lesson is the gospel itself. Humanity was banned from Eden for real cause, and the flaming sword was just. The good news is not that the ban was unfair but that the Son bore it — He was cast "without the gate" (Heb 13:12) so that the banned could come home. Tell your child that the one door God never shuts is the one Jesus opened.
roots_summary: Old English bannan (to proclaim, summon) → English ban (to forbid, curse) → gaming banned = removed by moderators → Gen Alpha’s ultimate threat.
roots_lines: Old English bannan — to summon, proclaim; Old Norse banna — to forbid, curse
Medieval ban — a proclamation, a curse, a sentence of outlawry
Internet forums (1990s): users banned by moderators
Game culture: perma-ban, temp-ban, ban hammer
Gen Alpha: "I’ll get you banned" as the ultimate playground threat
usage: "If you keep griefing my house I’m reporting you and you’ll get banned!"
Adam was banned from the garden; Christ was cast without the gate so the banned could come home (Heb 13:12).
Go to your brother first, not to the ban hammer (Mat 18:15).

etymology: Adopt Me!, a Roblox role-play game released in July 2017 by the studio later called Uplift Games. Players began as parents or babies adopting one another, then — from 2019 — as collectors adopting, raising, and trading pets hatched from eggs: dogs, unicorns, dragons, "neon" and "mega neon" versions made by combining four of the same pet. It drew more than a million players at once at its 2019–20 peak, and its pet-trading economy, with "legendary" pets valued like baseball cards, taught a generation the words trade, value, W or L, and scammer.
biblical_def: To a Gen Alpha child, Adopt Me is the Roblox game about raising pets and trading them, and "What’s your best pet in Adopt Me?" is a question about wealth. Kids spend hours caring for virtual pets, and more hours haggling over their value. The Christian observation: the game’s very name borrows one of the most beautiful words in the New Testament. Adoption is how God brings sinners into His family: "ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father" (Rom 8:15). God "predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself" (Eph 1:5) — not because we were the rare, valuable pet, but because He loved us. The game’s habit runs the other way: a pet is loved for what it is worth in trade, and a better one is always on offer. That is the very thing God’s adoption is not. He does not trade His children up. "When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up" (Psa 27:10). A father can tell a five-year-old: "In the game, people adopt pets and trade them for better ones. God adopted you, and He will never, ever trade you for anybody." And the nurturing play is worth praising: "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast" (Pro 12:10).
webster_summary: Roblox pet-raising and trading game (2017; pets from 2019) whose name borrows the gospel’s word for God’s family — a chance to teach the adoption that is never traded.
webster_full: ADOPT ME, proper n. (Roblox game, 2017–present; Gen Alpha usage) The pet-adopting, pet-raising, pet-trading role-play game. "I got a mega neon in Adopt Me!"
Vocabulary it spread: neon / mega neon (upgraded pets), legendary, trade value, W or L? (was that trade a win or loss?).
Decode for parents: the caring play is sweet; the trading economy is where scams, envy, and real-money side markets live.

Webster 1828, the root — ADOPT, v.t. To take a stranger into one’s family, as son and heir; to take one who is not a child, and treat him as one, giving him a title to the privileges and rights of a child.
scriptures: For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father.
Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will,
When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.
A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.
To redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons.
corruption_summary: Adopt Me borrows the gospel’s tenderest word and turns it into a market where every pet is loved for its trade value; God’s adoption is the opposite — unearned, unpriced, never traded.
corruption_paragraphs: The game’s double life is the lesson. Children do care for their pets, feeding and bathing them, and that nurture is good. But the economy rewards only rarity, so the beloved pet becomes an asset, and the trading screen becomes a school of envy and haggling. A child can learn there to measure love by market value.

Christ redeemed "them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons" (Gal 4:5). That adoption is a costly act of love toward the unworthy, sealed with blood, never revisited. Tell your child often that he is adopted into God’s family by grace, and that God’s children are not traded up. A game named Adopt Me can become a bedtime talk about Romans 8.
roots_summary: Latin adoptare (to choose for oneself) → English adopt → Adopt Me! (Roblox, 2017; pets 2019) → Gen Alpha’s pet-trading economy.
roots_lines: Latin ad + optare, to choose — to take a child as one’s own
Greek huiothesia — "placing as a son," Paul’s word for adoption (Rom 8:15; Eph 1:5)
July 2017: Adopt Me! released on Roblox as a family role-play
2019: pets and eggs added; neon and mega neon combining
2019–20: more than a million concurrent players; a trading economy with its own slang
usage: "Would you trade your frost dragon for my shadow dragon? W or L?"
In the game a pet is traded up; in the gospel the adopted child never is (Rom 8:15).
A righteous child regardeth the life of her beast — even a pixel puppy (Pro 12:10).

etymology: Brookhaven RP, a Roblox role-play town created by the developer Wolfpaq and released in April 2020, later run by Voldex. Players pick a house, a car, and a job, and act out ordinary life — families, schools, police chases, hospitals. It became the most-visited experience in Roblox history, with tens of billions of visits, and the most common place for Gen Alpha children to "play house" online — including with strangers who join their family.
biblical_def: Brookhaven is Gen Alpha’s online town: you get a house, a car, a job, and a family, and you pretend. It is playing house, the oldest game in the world, moved onto a server where anyone can knock on the door. Children role-play mom and dad, babies and teens, doctors and police — and the stories range from sweet to strange, because other children (and sometimes adults) write half the script. The Christian observation: the impulse to play house is God’s design showing through. Children rehearse the life they were made for — a home, a family, work — because God "setteth the solitary in families" (Psa 68:6) and made man to work and keep (Gen 2:15). That is worth honoring. But a pretend house with an unlocked door is not a home. Scripture says "Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it" (Psa 127:1), and a child’s play-family needs a real father’s eye on who comes in: "Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners" (1Co 15:33). A father can tell a five-year-old: "It’s fun to pretend to be a mommy or a daddy. In our family we only let real friends play house with us — and the best house is the one where Jesus lives."
webster_summary: Roblox’s most-visited role-play town (2020): playing house online — God’s design for home and work rehearsed in play, on a server whose door needs a father’s lock.
webster_full: BROOKHAVEN, proper n. (Roblox role-play game, 2020–present; Gen Alpha usage) The online town of houses, cars, jobs, and play-families. "Let’s do Brookhaven — I’ll be the mom."
Common play: family role-play, school, police and robbers, hospital, "adopting" other players as children.
Decode for parents: playing house is healthy; playing house with unknown strangers is where the risk lives. Use private servers and friends you know.

Webster 1828, the root — HAVEN, n. A harbor; a port; a bay, recess or inlet of the sea, or the mouth of a river which affords good anchorage and a safe station for ships; any place in which ships can be sheltered by the land from the force of tempests and a violent sea.
scriptures: God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains: but the rebellious dwell in a dry land.
A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.
Every wise woman buildeth her house: but the foolish plucketh it down with her hands.
corruption_summary: Brookhaven moves the holy game of playing house onto a public server; the instinct is God’s, but a house without walls invites guests a father would never let through the door.
corruption_paragraphs: Children have always rehearsed adulthood in play, and the rehearsal shapes them. When the rehearsal is co-written by anonymous strangers, the script can drift — toward drama, crude humor, "dating" role-plays, or adults seeking children. The danger is not the house; it is the open door, and the slow normalizing of strangers inside it.

Redeem the game by remembering what it imitates. "Every wise woman buildeth her house" (Pro 14:1); every godly father keeps his. Let your daughter play house with siblings and known friends, ask her about the stories she tells, and play along sometimes. Then point her to the real house the play anticipates: a family under God, where the LORD builds and the door is kept.
roots_summary: English brook + haven (place-name style) → Brookhaven RP (Roblox, 2020) → most-visited Roblox experience; Gen Alpha’s online play-house.
roots_lines: Old English broc (stream) + haefen (harbor, refuge)
April 2020: Brookhaven RP released on Roblox by Wolfpaq
Pandemic-era surge; later the most-visited Roblox experience
Play patterns: family role-play, school, police, hospital
usage: "Join my Brookhaven server — you can be my sister and we live in the big house."
Except the LORD build the house — even the pretend one — they labour in vain (Psa 127:1).
Playing house is a rehearsal for a family; keep strangers out of the rehearsal.

etymology: Blox Fruits, a Roblox action game released in 2019 by the studio Gamer Robot, modeled on the Japanese anime One Piece, in which "Devil Fruits" grant superpowers to whoever eats them. In Blox Fruits, players sail seas, grind levels, fight bosses, and hunt for fruits (Dragon, Leopard, Kitsune, Dough) that grant powers; rare fruits are traded and bought with Robux. It became one of Roblox’s most-played games, with tens of billions of visits, and "What fruit do you have?" became a playground status question.
biblical_def: In Blox Fruits you eat a magic fruit and gain a power — turn into a dragon, control light, become dough — then grind for hours to grow stronger. Gen Alpha boys especially talk about fruits the way earlier generations talked about baseball cards: "I got Leopard!" is a boast. The Christian observation: the game’s central image is a fruit that gives power to whoever takes it. That is precisely the serpent’s offer in Eden: "in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods" (Gen 3:5). Humanity has wanted a power-fruit ever since, and taking it was our ruin. Scripture’s answer is not a stronger fruit but a different kind of fruit altogether — the fruit the Spirit grows in us: "love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance" (Gal 5:22-23). Jesus did not grab power; He "took upon him the form of a servant" (Php 2:7). And the endless grind for levels can teach patience or devour time; "Redeeming the time" applies to sea-voyages too (Col 4:5). A father can tell a five-year-old: "In the story of Adam and Eve, a bad fruit promised power and made people sad. God gives us good fruit — like being kind and patient — and that’s the best power."
webster_summary: Roblox anime-style game (2019, after One Piece) of power-granting fruits and level-grinding — the serpent’s power-fruit in cartoon form, answered by the fruit of the Spirit.
webster_full: BLOX FRUITS, proper n. (Roblox game, 2019–present; Gen Alpha usage) The anime-style game in which eaten fruits grant powers. "I finally got Dragon in Blox Fruits."
Vocabulary: fruit (a power), awakening (upgrading it), grinding (repetitive leveling), sea (game region), raid.
Decode for parents: more violent and grindier than most Roblox staples; time is the main cost, and rare-fruit trading the main snare.
Webster 1828, the root — FRUIT, n. In a general sense, whatever the earth produces for the nourishment of animals, or for clothing or profit.
scriptures: For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,
Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.
But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:
Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time.
corruption_summary: Blox Fruits builds a game on the serpent’s offer — eat this and gain power — and trains hours of grinding toward it; Scripture answers with the Spirit’s fruit and the Son who did not grasp.
corruption_paragraphs: The premise is older than the anime: a fruit that makes you more than you are. Eden’s fruit was "to be desired to make one wise" (Gen 3:6), and its promise was power without obedience. A game cannot make a child sin by that premise, but it can make the premise feel like the shape of every good story — that the point of life is to become powerful, and the means is to acquire the right thing.

The Christian father can turn the game inside out. The fruit that matters is grown, not grabbed; it is character, not superpower; and the strongest Man who ever lived used His power to wash feet. Grind for that fruit, and the time is redeemed.
roots_summary: Japanese One Piece "Devil Fruits" (1997 manga) → Blox Fruits (Roblox, 2019) → playground status by fruit.
roots_lines: Latin fructus — enjoyment, produce → English fruit
1997: Eiichiro Oda’s One Piece introduces power-granting Devil Fruits
2019: Blox Fruits released on Roblox by Gamer Robot
Gen Alpha usage: "What fruit do you have?" as status question
Associated slang: grinding, awakening, raid, sea
usage: "Bro, trade me your Kitsune — I’ll give you Dough and two gamepasses."
The game’s fruit grants power; the Spirit’s fruit grants love, joy, peace (Gal 5:22).
Eden had a power-fruit too; that is where the trouble started (Gen 3:5).
